passages.source_text: καὶ δὴ μέλλουσιν ἡμῖν ἑστιᾶσθαι ὑπεισέδραμέ τις λέγων Ἀππίων ὁ πλειστονίκης σὺν Ἀννουβίωνι ἥκει ἀρτίως ἀπὸ Ἀντιοχείας καὶ ξενίζεται παρὰ Σίμωνι. ὁ δὲ πατὴρ ἀκούσας καὶ χαρεὶς ἔφη Πέτρῳ Εἴ μοι ἐπετρέπεις, πορεύομαι προσαγορεύσων Ἀππίωνα καὶ Ἀννουβίωνα ἐκ πρώτης ἡλικίας φίλους μοι γεγενημένους. τυχὸν γὰρ Ἀννουβίωνα πείσω Κλήμεντι διαλεχθῆναι περὶ γενέσεως. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐπιτρέπω, ἔφη, καὶ ἐπαινῶ τὰ φίλων σε πληροῦντα μέρη, πλὴν ἐννόει μοι ὡς κατὰ πρόνοιαν θεοῦ πανταχόθεν συντρέχει τὰ πρὸς τὴν σὴν πληροφορίαν οἰκείαν ἀποτελοῦντα τὴν ἁρμονίαν. τοῦτο δὲ εἶπον διὰ τὴν Ἀννουβίωνος χρησίμως σοι γενομένην ἐπιδημίαν. καὶ ὁ πατὴρ Ἀληθῶς συνορῶ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχον. καὶ ταῦτα εἰπὼν ἐπορεύθη πρὸς Σίμωνα.

ἡμεῖς δὲ οἱ συνόντες τῷ Πέτρῳ δι’ ὅλης νυκτὸς ἐπαλλήλως πυνθανόμενοι ὑπό τε ἡδονῆς καὶ χαρᾶς τῶν λεγομένων νήφοντες ἐνυκτερεύσαμεν. ἤδη δέ πως νυκτὸς ὑπαυγαζομένης, Πέτρος ἐμβλέψας ἐμοί τε καὶ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς μου ἔφη Διαπορῶ τί ἔδοξε τῷ ὑμετέρῳ πατρί. καὶ λέγοντος τοῦτο ἥκει ὁ πατὴρ αὐτόθι, τὸν Πέτρον ἡμῖν περὶ αὐτοῦ διαλεγόμενον καταλαβών· καὶ ἀθυμοῦντα ἰδὼν προσαγορεύσας ἀπελογήσατο δι’ ἣν αἰτίαν ἔξω κεκοίμηται. ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐμβλέποντες αὐτῷ ἐξειστήκειμεν, τὸ εἶδος Σίμωνος ὁρῶντες, φωνῆς δὲ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν ἀκούοντες Φαύστου. καὶ δὴ φευγόντων ἡμῶν αὐτὸν καὶ στυγούντων, ἐξεπέπληκτο ὁ πατὴρ ἐπὶ τῷ οὕτως ἀπηνῶς καὶ ἐχθρῶς αὐτῷ χρῆσθαι. μόνος δὲ Πέτρος τὴν κατὰ φύσιν αὐτοῦ ὁρῶν μορφὴν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἔφη Τίνος ἕνεκα βδελυσσόμενοι ἀπωθεῖσθε τὸν ὑμέτερον πατέρα; ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ ἡ μήτηρ ἔφαμεν Σίμων ἡμῖν οὗτος φαίνεται φωνὴν ἔχων τοῦ ἡμετέρου πατρός. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ὑμῖν μὲν ἡ ἀμάγευτος αὐτοῦ φωνὴ μόνη γνώριμός ἐστιν, ἐμοῦ δὲ τοῖς ἀμαγεύτοις ὀφθαλμοῖς καὶ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ὡς ἔστιν ὁρατὸν ὅτι μὴ ἔστι Σίμων, ἀλλὰ Φαῦστος ὁ ὑμέτερος πατήρ. τότε δὴ προσεμβλέψας καὶ τῷ πατρὶ ἔφη ......... όν σου εἶδος αὐτοῖς οὐ φαίνεται, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνος τοῦ ἀσεβεστάτου καὶ ἡμῖν .........

ταῦτα τοῦ Πέτρου διαλεγομένου ἐπεισῄει τις τῶν προόδων ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας ........... λέγων Πέτρῳ Εἰδέναι σε θέλω, κύριέ μου, ὅτι Σίμων ἐν τῇ Ἀντιοχείᾳ δημοσίᾳ πολλὰ τεράστια ποιῶν μάγον σε ὀνομάζων καὶ γόητα πρὸς τοσοῦτον αὐτοὺς μῖσος παρεσκεύασεν ὡς γλίχεσθαι πάντα ἄνθρωπον τῶν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημησάντων σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου. ὅθεν ἡμεῖς οἱ πρόοδοι μετὰ τῶν ὑπὸ σοῦ τῷ Σίμωνι ὑποβεβλημένων ἀδελφῶν ἡμῶν πολὺ κατὰ σοῦ βρύχουσαν τὴν πόλιν ἑωρακότες, κρύφα εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ γενόμενοι σκοποῦμεν τί χρὴ ποιεῖν. καὶ δὴ ἐν ἀπορίᾳ ἡμῶν ὄντων ἐπεδήμησε Κορνήλιος ἑκατόνταρχος ὑπὸ Καίσαρος πεμφθεὶς πρὸς τὸν τῆς ἐπαρχίας ἡγούμενον, ὃν ἐν Καισαρείᾳ δαιμονῶντα ἰάσατο ὁ κύριος. οὗτος μεταπεμφθεὶς ὑφ’ ἡμῶν κρύφα καὶ τῆς ἀθυμίας τὴν αἰτίαν παρ’ ἡμῶν μαθὼν καὶ βοηθεῖν ἀξιωθεὶς προθυμότατα ὑπέσχετο φοβήσας φυγαδεύειν αὐτόν. ἐάν γε αὐτοῦ τῷ ἐγχειρήματι ὑπουργήσωμεν. ἡμῶν δὲ ἑτοίμως πάντα ποιήσειν ὑποσχομένων ἔφη Ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν φίλων κρύφα εἰς σύλληψιν αὐτοῦ ἐληλυθέναι περισκοποῦντος καὶ ζητεῖν αὐτὸν φάσκοντος, καθότι Καῖσαρ πολλοὺς μάγους ἀνελὼν καὶ τὰ κατ’ αὐτὸν μαθὼν ἐμὲ ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ ζήτησιν ἔπεμψεν, ὅπως καὶ αὐτὸν ὡς καὶ τοὺς πρὸ αὐτοῦ μάγους κολάσῃ. καὶ οἱ ὑμέτεροι οἱ συνόντες αὐτῷ ὡς δὴ κρύφα ποθὲν ἀκηκοότες προσαναφερέτωσαν ὡς ἐμοῦ ἕνεκα τοῦ συλλαβεῖν αὐτὸν ἀπεσταλμένου, καὶ τυχὸν ἀκούσας φοβηθεὶς φεύξεται. ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ἕτερόν τι ποιεῖν ἐπενοήσαμεν, ὅμως οὕτως ἐγένετο. ὑπό τε γὰρ πολλῶν τῶν ἔξω εἰς τὰ μεγάλα αὐτῷ χαριζομένων λάθρα λεγόντων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τῶν ἔνδον ὑποβλητῶν ἡμετέρων ἀκηκοὼς καὶ ὡς παρ’ ἰδίων γνώμην εἰληφὼς ὑποστέλλεσθαι ἔγνω. ἀποδρὰς οὖν τῆς Ἀντιοχείας μετὰ Ἀθηνοδώρου ἐνθάδε ἐλήλυθεν ὡς ἀκηκόαμεν. διὸ συμβουλεύομέν σοι μήπω ἐπιβῆναι τῆς πόλεως ἐκείνης, μέχρις ἂν εἰδῶμεν εἰ τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται.

ταῦτα τοῦ προόδου ἀπαγγείλαντος, ὁ Πέτρος τῷ πατρὶ προσεμβλέψας ἔφη Ἀκούεις, Φαῦστε, ὑπὸ Σίμωνος τοῦ μάγου ἡ μεταμόρφωσίς σου γέγονεν, ὡς ἤδη φαίνεται. Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν φοβηθεὶς ἔφυγε, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σοὶ περιθεὶς μορφήν, ὅπως ἀποθανόντος σου τοῖς σοῖς τέκνοις ἡ λύπη γένηται. ταῦτα ὁ πατὴρ ἀκούων κλαίων καὶ ὀδυρόμενος ἔφη Ὀρθῶς ἐστοχάσω, Πέτρε. Ἀννουβίων ...... μού με φιλῶν μυστηριωδῶς τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν ἐξέφηγε, καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος.

ταῦτα τοῦ πατρὸς εἰπόντος μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ ....... πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὴν Σίμωνος ἡμῖν δηλῶν φυγὴν καὶ ὡς αὐτῆς νυκτὸς ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίαν ὥρμησεν. εὗρε δὲ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν κοπτόμενον καὶ μετὰ ὀδυρμῶν λέγοντα Οἴμοι ὁ τάλας, μάγον αὐτὸν ἀκούων ἠπίστουν ὁ ταλαίπωρος· πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπιγνωσθεὶς συμβίῳ καὶ τέκνοις ταχέως ἐπὶ τὴν προτέραν τῆς ἀγνοίας ἦλθον συμφοράν. καὶ ἡ μήτηρ ὀδυρομένη τὰς τρίχας κατέτιλλεν, ἡμεῖς δὲ περὶ τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς ἀλλοιώσεως ἀδημονοῦντες ἐστένομεν, ὅ,τι ποτὲ ἦν συννοῆσαι μὴ δυνάμενοι. Ἀννουβίων δὲ ταῦτα ἀκούων καὶ ὁρῶν ἀχανὴς ἔστη. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἡμῖν τοῖς τέκνοις ἐπὶ πάντων ἔφη Πιστεύσατέ μοι, οὗτός ἐστι Φαῦστος ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν. διὸ δὴ κελεύω ὑμῖν ὡς πατρὶ προσέχειν· παρέξει γὰρ ὁ θεὸς πρόφασίν τινα, δι᾽ ἧς τὴν Σίμωνος ἀποδυσάμενος μορφὴν τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν προδήλως ἀναδείξει πάλιν. ταῦτα ἡμῖν εἰπὼν καὶ τῷ πατρὶ προσβλέψας ἔφη Ἐγώ σοι ἐπέτρεψα προσαγορεῦσαι Ἀππίωνα καὶ Ἀννουβίωνα, ἐπειδὴ ἐκ παίδων σοι φίλους εἶναι ὁμολογεῖς, οὐχὶ Σίμωνι τῷ μάγῳ συνομιλεῖν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: Just as a meal was about to be served to us, someone slipped in and said, “Appion the Many-Victor has just arrived from Antioch with Annoubion and is staying as Simon’s guest.” When our father heard this, he rejoiced and said to Peter, “If you permit me, I will go greet Appion and Annoubion, who have been my friends from earliest youth. Perhaps I may persuade Annoubion to debate Clement about nativity.” Peter said, “I permit it, and I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship. But consider how, by God’s providence, everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony. I say this because Annoubion’s arrival has proved advantageous to you.” Our father replied, “I truly see that this is so.” After saying this, he went to Simon.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀππίων ὁ πλειστονίκης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Appion the Many-Victor
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet denoting numerous victories rather than silently transliterated as another personal name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ γενέσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: about nativity
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this debate setting γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, particularly as a subject of astrological determinism; “birth” or “genesis” remains possible more generally.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπαινῶ τὰ φίλων σε πληροῦντα μέρη
lexical_decisions.chosen: I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom describes performing the part or duties belonging to friends; the English avoids reproducing the awkward literal image of “parts.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πανταχόθεν συντρέχει τὰ πρὸς τὴν σὴν πληροφορίαν οἰκείαν ἀποτελοῦντα τὴν ἁρμονίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκείαν is taken with τὴν ἁρμονίαν as “fitting”; attachment to πληροφορίαν, yielding something like “your own assurance,” is also grammatically possible.

passages.text: As for us who were with Peter, we spent the whole night asking questions one after another, remaining awake because of the pleasure and joy produced by what was being said. When the night was already beginning somehow to brighten, Peter looked at me and my brothers and said, “I am perplexed about what your father decided.” While he was saying this, our father arrived there and found Peter discussing him with us. Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained why he had slept outside. We stared at him in astonishment, seeing Simon’s appearance but hearing the voice of our father Faustus. As we recoiled from him and regarded him with loathing, our father was astounded at being treated so harshly and hostilely by us. Only Peter, who saw his natural form, said to us, “Why do you push your father away in disgust?” We and our mother replied, “To us this man looks like Simon, though he has our father’s voice.” Peter said, “For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes his appearance too is visible as it really is: he is not Simon but Faustus, your father.” Then, looking directly at our father too, he said, “......... appearance of yours is not visible to them, but Simon’s—the most impious man’s—is; and to us .........”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: νήφοντες ἐνυκτερεύσαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we spent the whole night ... remaining awake
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here νήφω concerns wakeful alertness during the night rather than literal abstinence from intoxication; “remaining clear-minded” is possible but less closely fitted to the overnight setting.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἀθυμοῦντα ἰδὼν προσαγορεύσας ἀπελογήσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unexpressed person seen as disheartened is taken to be Peter, whom the arriving father has just found discussing him. Reference to another participant is formally possible but less natural in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μόνος δὲ Πέτρος τὴν κατὰ φύσιν αὐτοῦ ὁρῶν μορφὴν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Only Peter, who saw his natural form
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ φύσιν identifies the form belonging to Faustus’s real nature, in contrast to the magically imposed appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ὑμῖν μὲν ἡ ἀμάγευτος αὐτοῦ φωνὴ μόνη γνώριμός ἐστιν, ἐμοῦ δὲ τοῖς ἀμαγεύτοις ὀφθαλμοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμάγευτος is rendered as freedom from magical alteration or deception, preserving the repetition applied first to the voice and then to Peter’s eyes.

source_issues.source_quote: ......... όν σου εἶδος αὐτοῖς οὐ φαίνεται, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνος τοῦ ἀσεβεστάτου καὶ ἡμῖν .........
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints two lacunae of nine dots each. After the first gap, only όν survives, either as an isolated form or as the ending of a lost word, and it cannot receive a secure independent English rendering. Both nine-dot gaps remain explicit, and no restoration of either gap or of the broken construction is supplied.

passages.text: While Peter was saying this, one of the advance messengers came in from Antioch ..........., saying to Peter, “I want you to know, my lord, that Simon, by publicly performing many marvels in Antioch and calling you a magician and a sorcerer, has stirred them to such hatred that every person among those staying there longs to taste your very flesh. Consequently, when we advance messengers and our brothers whom you had planted with Simon saw the city gnashing furiously against you, we met secretly in one place to consider what must be done. While we were at a loss, Cornelius arrived, a centurion sent by Caesar to the governor of the province—the man whom the Lord had healed at Caesarea when he was demon-possessed. We summoned him secretly, explained the reason for our discouragement, and appealed to him for help. He very eagerly promised to frighten Simon into flight, provided, of course, that we assisted him in his undertaking. When we readily promised to do everything, he said, ‘While I keep watch and secretly claim through many friends that I have come to arrest him and am searching for him—because Caesar has executed many magicians, learned the facts about him, and sent me to seek him so that he might punish him just like the magicians before him—let your people who are with him also report, as though they had secretly heard it somewhere, that I have been sent to arrest him. Perhaps when he hears it, he will take fright and flee.’ Now although we had considered doing something else, this is nevertheless what happened. For after he had heard it from many outsiders—who secretly told him while currying his favor in important matters—and also from our planted agents inside, and had received what he took to be advice from his own people, he decided to withdraw. He therefore escaped from Antioch and, as we have heard, came here with Athenodorus. We consequently advise you not yet to enter that city, until we know whether, with him absent, they will be able to recover from his slander against you.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τις τῶν προόδων
lexical_decisions.chosen: one of the advance messengers
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόοδοι denotes people who go ahead or operate in advance; “forerunners” is possible but less clear in this organizational context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλὰ τεράστια ποιῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: performing many marvels
lexical_decisions.rationale: τεράστια denotes extraordinary, portent-like feats; “wonders” or, with a hostile nuance, “monstrous feats” are alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μάγον σε ὀνομάζων καὶ γόητα
lexical_decisions.chosen: calling you a magician and a sorcerer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two accusations are kept distinct. γόης can also mean “conjurer,” “charlatan,” or “impostor,” but the magical context supports “sorcerer.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου
lexical_decisions.chosen: to taste your very flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτῶν is taken intensively with σαρκῶν, heightening the violent image; a strictly reflexive reference to the flesh of some other group is less natural here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἐν Καισαρείᾳ δαιμονῶντα ἰάσατο ὁ κύριος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the man whom the Lord had healed at Caesarea when he was demon-possessed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes ὅν as referring to Cornelius. Because the provincial governor is the nearer masculine antecedent, reference to the governor is grammatically possible and remains an alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν φίλων κρύφα εἰς σύλληψιν αὐτοῦ ἐληλυθέναι περισκοποῦντος καὶ ζητεῖν αὐτὸν φάσκοντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: While I keep watch and secretly claim through many friends that I have come to arrest him and am searching for him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive construction presents Cornelius as maintaining surveillance while causing or allowing the claim to circulate through friends. The precise attachment of διὰ πολλῶν φίλων and κρύφα is flexible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἔξω εἰς τὰ μεγάλα αὐτῷ χαριζομένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: outsiders ... currying his favor in important matters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is understood as describing outsiders who seek Simon’s favor in substantial affairs; “who did him great favors” is another viable rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς παρ’ ἰδίων γνώμην εἰληφὼς ὑποστέλλεσθαι ἔγνω
lexical_decisions.chosen: having received what he took to be advice from his own people, he decided to withdraw
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this receive-from construction, γνώμη is taken as “advice” or “counsel,” distinguishing it from merely hearing the report. The broader senses “judgment” or “information” remain possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: with him absent, they will be able to recover from his slander against you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context calls for abatement of, or recovery from, the effects of Simon’s slander. The exact lexical force of the printed ὑπολῆσαι remains uncertain.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints an eleven-dot lacuna between “from Antioch” and “saying to Peter.” The missing wording is unavailable; all eleven dots are retained, and no identity, description, or adverb is restored.

The edition reads ὑπολῆσαι, which is lexically irregular in this construction. A possible regularization is ὑπολῆξαι, with ξ in place of σ, understood as “cease” or “abate.” That regularization is conjectural; the English follows a contextual interpretation of the printed wording and does not present the conjecture as the supplied reading.

passages.text: When the advance messenger had reported these things, Peter looked directly at our father and said, “Do you hear, Faustus? Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician, as is now evident. Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm, he fled in fear, placing his own form upon you so that, when you died, grief would come upon your children.” Hearing this, our father wept and lamented, saying, “You have judged correctly, Peter. Annoubion ...... of mine, because he loved me, cryptically disclosed the plot, and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ Σίμωνος τοῦ μάγου ἡ μεταμόρφωσίς σου γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction presents Simon as the agent responsible for Faustus’s altered appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπὶ κακῷ indicates harmful or punitive intent without specifying the precise punishment. The contextual interpretation of Caesar as the seeker is retained despite the printed case irregularity disclosed in source_issues.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σοὶ περιθεὶς μορφήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: placing his own form upon you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete image of putting Simon’s appearance around or upon Faustus is retained rather than reduced to simple resemblance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μυστηριωδῶς τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν ἐξέφηγε
lexical_decisions.chosen: cryptically disclosed the plot
lexical_decisions.rationale: μυστηριωδῶς indicates an indirect, mysterious, or cryptic disclosure; ἐπιβουλή is a hostile plot or design.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος
lexical_decisions.chosen: and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first-person speaker and the following first-person ἤμην support “I,” but the precise ending of ἐπίστευ- and any further lost wording remain unavailable. The English does not supply an object of belief.

source_issues.source_quote: Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν
source_issues.issue: The edition prints the genitive Καίσαρος, although the contextual reading takes Caesar as the subject of ζητεῖν, for which the accusative Καίσαρα would ordinarily be expected in this infinitival construction after νομίσας. Καίσαρα is only a proposed grammatical regularization; the translation retains the contextually defensible interpretation without claiming that the regularization is printed.

The selected edition prints a six-dot lacuna before μού. The surviving “of mine” indicates a lost description or relationship, but its wording cannot be recovered. All six dots remain explicit, and no description is restored.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints ten dots immediately after the surviving verbal stem ἐπίστευ-. The precise verbal ending and any following words are unavailable; the ten-dot gap is retained without supplying an object or other lost content.

passages.text: After our father said this, not long afterward ....... to us, reporting Simon’s flight to us and that he had set out for Judea that very night. He found our father beating himself and saying with lamentation, “Alas, wretch that I am! Though I heard that he was a magician, miserable man that I am, I refused to believe it. After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day, I quickly returned to my former calamity of being unknown.” Our mother, lamenting, kept tearing out her hair, while we groaned in distress over our father’s alteration, unable to understand what on earth it was. When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed. Before everyone, Peter said to us children, “Believe me: this is Faustus, your father. I therefore command you to pay him the regard due to a father, for God will provide some occasion through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again.” After saying this to us, he looked at our father and said, “I permitted you to greet Appion and Annoubion because you acknowledge that they have been your friends since childhood, not to associate with Simon the magician.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὗρε δὲ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν κοπτόμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: He found our father beating himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόπτομαι can describe striking oneself as an embodied act of mourning; the accompanying lament supports retaining that concrete action.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπιγνωσθεὶς συμβίῳ καὶ τέκνοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιγινώσκω here concerns recognition of identity, while σύμβιος denotes one’s spouse or life-partner; the context identifies Faustus’s wife.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν προτέραν τῆς ἀγνοίας ἦλθον συμφοράν
lexical_decisions.chosen: I returned to my former calamity of being unknown
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγνοία is understood contextually as his family’s failure to recognize him, not merely as intellectual ignorance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀννουβίων δὲ ταῦτα ἀκούων καὶ ὁρῶν ἀχανὴς ἔστη
lexical_decisions.chosen: When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀχανής preserves the visible image of standing open-mouthed in stunned astonishment; “stood aghast” or “stood dumbfounded” conveys the reaction but not the image as directly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς πατρὶ προσέχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to pay him the regard due to a father
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσέχειν calls for attention, adherence, or care toward Faustus in his paternal identity; “attend to him as a father” is more literal but less idiomatic.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δι᾽ ἧς τὴν Σίμωνος ἀποδυσάμενος μορφὴν τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν προδήλως ἀναδείξει πάλιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes Faustus as the understood subject of “stripping off” and “revealing,” since the middle image naturally depicts him shedding Simon’s form. The nearest explicit subject is God, so taking God as the agent of the removal and revelation is grammatically possible, though less natural with the stripping image.

source_issues.source_quote: μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ ....... πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὴν Σίμωνος ἡμῖν δηλῶν φυγὴν
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a seven-dot lacuna after “not long afterward.” The missing subject and finite expression governing “to us” are unavailable. All seven dots remain explicit, and the arriving reporter is not identified.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
